segments.say: Nadia thinks back to the beginning of the evening, before the teapot. Her friend Sam had told a long story about a meeting at work, and at the end, everyone had laughed politely. It was a friendly laugh, but it was nothing like the helpless laughter later on. Even at the time, everyone at the table could probably hear the difference.

Researchers often separate laughter into two broad kinds. One is spontaneous: the laugh that bursts out of us before we've decided anything, like the teapot laughter. The other is volitional, a laugh we choose to make, often to be polite, to show agreement or to keep a conversation friendly. Both are real behaviour. But they're produced somewhat differently.

In 2005, the researchers Matthew Gervais and David Sloan Wilson published a long review of laughter research. They argued that these two kinds of laughter have different histories. The spontaneous kind, they suggested, is the older one, rooted in the play signals we met earlier. The chosen kind may have developed later, as humans gained more control over their faces and voices.

show.who: Matthew Gervais and David Sloan Wilson
show.what: The evolution and functions of laughter and humor: a synthetic approach

segments.say: There's support for this from brain research. Spontaneous laughter seems to depend heavily on older brain systems involved in emotion, while posed or chosen laughter depends more on areas that control deliberate movements, like speaking. That's one reason why a forced laugh can sound a little stiff. It's being produced by a different set of controls.

In a brain-imaging study published in 2015, Carolyn McGettigan, Sophie Scott and colleagues played volunteers recordings of real laughter, produced while watching funny videos, and posed laughter, produced on request. The volunteers were simply asked to listen. The brain treated the two differently, even when the listeners weren't asked to judge them.

show.who: Carolyn McGettigan, Sophie Scott and colleagues
show.what: Individual differences in laughter perception reveal roles for mentalizing and sensorimotor systems in the evaluation of emotional authenticity

segments.say: Posed laughter, in particular, activated brain areas involved in thinking about other people's minds, as if the listener's brain was asking, why is this person laughing, what do they mean by it? Real laughter didn't need that extra work as much. It seemed to be understood more directly, as a simple sign of amusement.

Can people tell the two kinds apart? In 2018, Gregory Bryant and a large team of colleagues tested this around the world, in 21 different societies, from big cities to small rural communities. Listeners heard short recordings of laughs and were asked whether each one was real or fake. Their task was simply to guess.

show.what: The perception of spontaneous and volitional laughter across 21 societies

segments.say: Across all those societies, listeners did better than chance at telling spontaneous laughs from posed ones. They weren't perfect, but the ability appeared everywhere, in every kind of community. It seems that recognising a genuine laugh is a widely shared human skill, not something learned from one particular culture or language.

Researchers have pointed to some of the features that set spontaneous laughter apart. It tends to be higher in pitch and more irregular. It's often breathier and sounds less controlled, as if the voice has been taken over. And its bursts can come faster than in posed laughter. In short, a real laugh sounds like it happened to the person, rather than being made by them.

show.title: How real laughs tend to sound

segments.say: A table with two small candles burning beside a pair of empty teacups and a folded napkin, the light catching the rims of the cups. It's a reminder of the many small social moments in an evening with friends. Not every laugh at a table like this is helpless. Many are gentle and chosen, and they matter too.

show.cap: Candles and teacups on a table

segments.say: It's important not to think of chosen laughter as dishonest. A polite laugh is often a kindness. It tells the speaker, I'm listening, I'm with you, I appreciate you sharing this. Sam's work story might not have been hilarious, but the friendly laughter at the end said, we're glad you told us. That's a perfectly good reason to laugh.

There's evidence, too, that the sound of laughter itself is understood across very different cultures. In 2010, Disa Sauter and colleagues played recordings of emotional sounds, like screams, sighs and laughter, to members of the Himba community in northern Namibia, who had very little contact with Western culture, and to British listeners.

show.who: Disa Sauter, Frank Eisner, Paul Ekman and Sophie Scott
show.where: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2010
show.what: Cross-cultural recognition of basic emotions through nonverbal emotional vocalizations

segments.say: Laughter was among the sounds that both groups recognised best in each other's recordings. Himba listeners recognised the laughter of British speakers, and British listeners recognised Himba laughter. Some other emotional sounds, by contrast, were harder to recognise across cultures. Laughter, it seems, is one of the most universal sounds we make.

A note of caution, as always. Most of these studies use short recordings, heard without the context of a real conversation. In everyday life, we have faces, situations and history to help us. So these experiments probably underestimate how well we read laughter in person, and also miss how often we simply don't notice whether a laugh is chosen or not.

So here's what we can say. There seem to be two broad kinds of laughter, spontaneous and chosen. Brains treat them a little differently. People around the world can often tell them apart, better than chance. And laughter as a sound is recognised across very different cultures. It's one of the clearest signals in the human repertoire.

show.title: What we can say
items: There are spontaneous and chosen laughs
People everywhere can often tell them apart

segments.say: Nadia realises that both kinds of laughter had their place tonight. The polite laughter at Sam's story kept the conversation warm and made Sam feel heard. The helpless laughter at the teapot made everyone feel like students again. One was chosen, one wasn't, and both were, in their own way, gifts to each other.

And that raises another question. If people can hear whether a laugh is real, can they also hear something about the people laughing? Could a stranger, listening to a recording of two people laughing together, tell whether they're old friends or people who have only just met? Some researchers tried exactly that.
